passage: At the Saturday maths club, Sunaina ma'am held up Vikas's worksheet. "Look, all correct again! Vikas is our little genius." The others clapped. Then she put two stacks on the table: easy puzzles and a new "challenge" set. "Pick whichever you like." Vikas picked the easy ones. He finished in ten minutes and sat drawing. When Meena from his class tried to hand him a challenge puzzle, he pushed it back so hard the paper tore. "I don't want it!" Sunaina ma'am was surprised. At the end she asked him quietly why. Vikas looked at his shoes. "If I get it wrong, then I'm not a genius anymore."

qa.q: What did Sunaina ma'am call Vikas when she held up his worksheet?
qa.a: "Our little genius."

qa.q: Why did Vikas push the challenge puzzle away so angrily?
qa.a: He was scared that getting it wrong would take away the "genius" label; the anger covered his fear of losing it.

qa.q: What could Sunaina ma'am try next time instead of calling him a genius?
qa.a: Praise the way he worked through a problem, and celebrate trying a hard puzzle even if it's wrong, so risk feels safe.

qa.q: How might Meena have felt when the puzzle was pushed back?
qa.a: Meena was trying to share and may have felt hurt or confused by the sudden anger, not knowing it came from fear.

grounding: A child praised as a genius avoids challenging puzzles to protect the label.

passage: I'm Deepak, Mahima's older brother. Since she started reading at four, every relative has called her "our brilliant girl". Nani says it, our uncles say it, Papa says it at every dinner. Lately I've noticed something. When I set up the chess board, Mahima says she's busy. She used to love chess, but last month I beat her twice. She rereads easy storybooks she has already finished instead of the thick one her teacher gave her. Yesterday I asked her to try a crossword with me and she snapped, "I don't like stupid games!" and stomped off. I don't know for sure what's going on in her head. But she only seems to do things she already knows she'll win.

qa.q: What does every relative call Mahima?
qa.a: "Our brilliant girl."

qa.q: What might Mahima be afraid of when she refuses chess and the crossword?
qa.a: She may fear that losing or struggling would prove she isn't brilliant after all, so avoiding hard things protects the label everyone gives her.

qa.q: How could the family's praise change to help Mahima take risks?
qa.a: Praising her effort and the ways she tries, like working out a crossword clue, rather than calling her brilliant, so struggling doesn't feel like failing.

qa.q: How does Deepak feel about the change in his sister?
qa.a: Deepak seems puzzled and a little worried, missing the sister who loved chess, and unsure what is going on inside her.

grounding: An older brother notices his sister, always called brilliant, avoiding any challenge she might not win.

passage:
Monday, first week of term: Chinmay solved the class puzzle first. "You're so smart, Chinmay," the teacher said. Eshaan, next to him, whispered, "Show-off." Chinmay glowed all day.
Thursday, three weeks later: The teacher offered a "tough question" to anyone who wanted extra points. Eshaan tried and got it half right. Chinmay kept his hand down. At home he told his mother the question was boring.
Saturday, a month later: The science quiz had a new kind of problem. Chinmay stared at it, face hot, and left it blank rather than guess. When Eshaan asked how he'd done, he snapped, "Leave me alone!" and walked off. That night he whispered to his mother, "What if I'm not actually smart?"

qa.q: What did the teacher say when Chinmay solved the puzzle first?
qa.a: "You're so smart, Chinmay."

qa.q: What was Chinmay worried about when he whispered to his mother?
qa.a: That struggling with the new problem meant he wasn't really smart; the label had become something he could lose, so every hard question felt like a threat.

qa.q: What went wrong over the month, and what could help Chinmay now?
qa.a: Praise for being smart made him avoid risk; praise for trying new methods, and a calm talk about mistakes being part of learning, could help.

qa.q: How might Eshaan see Chinmay's change over the month?
qa.a: Eshaan saw a show-off at first, then a classmate who won't try and snaps at him, and may feel confused or hurt.

grounding: Over a month, a child praised as smart begins avoiding hard questions to protect the label.

passage: Dhruv, your Nani tells me you won't touch the puzzle book I sent, only the easy colouring one. Come, sit with your old Manoj Nana. When I was nine, everyone in our house called me "the clever one". "Manoj is so smart," at every wedding, every festival. I loved it. But here's the funny thing: I started running from hard sums. If the teacher put a tricky question on the board, I pretended not to see it. If I got it wrong, they'd find out I wasn't clever after all. My cousin, whom nobody called clever, tried everything and got stuck all the time, and by twelve he was better at maths than me. Being "the clever one" felt like carrying a glass bowl. I was so scared of dropping it that I stopped walking.

qa.q: What did everyone in the house call young Manoj?
qa.a: 'The clever one.'

qa.q: Why did young Manoj pretend not to see tricky questions?
qa.a: He feared a wrong answer would prove he wasn't clever after all; protecting the label made trying feel dangerous.

qa.q: What could the family have praised instead, and how might that have changed things?
qa.a: His trying and his methods rather than his cleverness; then getting stuck wouldn't threaten who he was, and hard sums would feel safe to attempt.

qa.q: What might Dhruv realise about the puzzle book after this story?
qa.a: Dhruv might see that avoiding the puzzle book protects a label, and that trying and getting stuck, as the cousin did, is how people get better.

grounding: A grandfather recalls how being called clever as a child made him avoid hard problems to protect the label.

passage: The inter-school quiz in Bhopal started late because a bus broke down, so each team had only two minutes to choose a round: "Easy Picks", or the "Challenge Round" for double points. Jeevan, ten, had heard "You're our little genius" from his mother, Rashmi, every day since he could read. She'd said it again that morning at the gate. His teammates wanted the Challenge Round. Jeevan's stomach clenched. What if he got one wrong, up on the stage, with Mummy in the second row? "Easy Picks," he insisted, so firmly that the others gave in. They won the easy round easily. On the bus home, Rashmi said, "My genius!" Jeevan stared out of the window and didn't answer. He wasn't sure why he felt worse, not better.

qa.q: Why did each team have only two minutes to choose a round?
qa.a: The inter-school quiz started late because a bus broke down.

qa.q: Why did Jeevan's stomach clench at the idea of the Challenge Round?
qa.a: He feared getting one wrong on stage in front of his mother and losing the 'genius' label 😰, so the harder round felt dangerous.

qa.q: What could Rashmi say on the bus to make challenge feel safer next time?
qa.a: Praise the effort and teamwork, and say she'd be proud of him for trying the harder round even if they got some wrong.

qa.q: How might Jeevan's teammates see his insistence on Easy Picks?
qa.a: They wanted the Challenge Round and might feel let down or puzzled, not knowing that the 'genius' label made him afraid of a single mistake.

grounding: A child constantly called a genius avoids the harder quiz round to keep the label, and the praise leaves him uneasy.

passage: In the village school near Hubli, everyone called Swati "the clever one." Urmila teacher said it when she finished sums first. Her grandmother said it to the neighbours. At the school fair, there was a new puzzle table with wooden shapes to fit into a box. Swati watched a small boy struggle with it. "Try it, Swati! You're so clever!" Urmila teacher called. Swati's stomach tightened. What if she couldn't? She said, "It's for small kids," and walked to the bangle stall. Later, when her friend teased her that she was scared, Swati snapped, "I'm not!" and stamped off. She sat behind the stalls, kicking the dust, cheeks hot.

qa.q: What was on the new puzzle table?
qa.a: Wooden shapes to fit into a box.

qa.q: Why did Swati's stomach tighten when she was told to try the puzzle?
qa.a: She was afraid that if she couldn't solve it, she would lose the label of 'the clever one', so trying felt risky.

qa.q: How could Urmila teacher encourage Swati differently?
qa.a: She could praise Swati's effort and trying new ways, rather than calling her clever, so a hard puzzle feels safe to attempt.

qa.q: How might Swati's friend see her walking away?
qa.a: Her friend may think she is scared or proud, not knowing she is protecting the 'clever' label.

grounding: It shows a child repeatedly called clever who avoids a hard puzzle to keep that label, becoming angry when teased.

passage: In Lisbon, Gabriel's grandmother Jana told everyone he was a genius. He had learned chess at six, and at nine he beat most of his classmates. "So smart," she said at every family lunch. At the chess club, the coach laid out a tricky endgame puzzle for the older children and invited Gabriel to try. He looked at it and felt his face go hot. "I'll do the easy ones," he said, sliding back to the beginner table. At home, he stopped playing against his grandmother's friend, who sometimes beat him. When Jana asked why, he threw his pieces back into the box. "It's boring." Later, alone, he set up the endgame puzzle on his board, stared at it, and put it away without moving a piece.

qa.q: Where did Gabriel slide back to at the chess club?
qa.a: The beginner table.

qa.q: Why did Gabriel feel his face go hot when invited to try the endgame puzzle?
qa.a: He felt anxious about failing in front of others and losing the 'genius' label, so avoiding it felt safer.

qa.q: What could the coach or Jana say to make hard puzzles feel less dangerous?
qa.a: They could praise his thinking and practice, like 'you tried three ideas', instead of calling him smart, so mistakes feel normal.

qa.q: How might Jana feel when Gabriel throws the pieces in the box?
qa.a: Jana may feel confused and hurt, not realising that her praise makes him afraid of losing.

grounding: It shows a child who is always called smart and starts avoiding hard chess problems and strong opponents to protect that label.

passage: At the Saturday maths club in the community centre, Tarun sir always introduced Pooja the same way: "Our little genius." Pooja, eleven, smiled every time. This week he put up a hard olympiad problem and said, "Pooja, you'll crack this in two minutes." Everyone turned to look. Pooja stared at the board. She didn't know where to start. Her hands went cold. "I have a headache," she said, and asked to sit out. Later, when another girl solved it after several wrong tries, the class clapped. Pooja clenched her pencil hard enough to snap the lead. On the bus home, she told her mother she didn't want to go to maths club anymore. "It's too easy," she said, looking out of the window.

qa.q: What did Tarun sir call Pooja?
qa.a: Our little genius.

qa.q: Why did Pooja say she had a headache?
qa.a: She felt scared of failing in front of everyone after being called a genius, so sitting out felt safer than trying and getting it wrong.

qa.q: How could Tarun sir change his praise to help Pooja?
qa.a: He could praise the effort and different methods students try, so Pooja sees wrong tries as part of learning.

qa.q: How might the girl who solved the problem see Pooja's reaction?
qa.a: She might not notice or might think Pooja is upset with her, without knowing Pooja fears losing her label.

grounding: It shows a child repeatedly called a genius who avoids a hard problem to protect the label, feeling angry and pulling away.

passage:
Monday: At the parents' meeting, Thomas Sir said, “Vasudha is so clever. A natural at maths.” Vasudha glowed all the way home.
Wednesday: In class, Sir gave the Olympiad puzzle sheet to anyone who wanted it. Vasudha didn't take one. What if she couldn't do them? Then she wouldn't be the clever one anymore. She did the easy textbook sums instead, fast and perfect.
Friday: Her friend Mira was struggling with a puzzle and asked for help. Vasudha looked at it, didn't see the answer at once, and snapped, “It's a stupid question.” She went red and walked off.
At home she was cross all evening. When Amma asked why, she said, “I don't like puzzles.” She didn't say she was scared of being not clever.

qa.q: What did Thomas Sir say about Vasudha at the parents' meeting?
qa.a: He said, “Vasudha is so clever. A natural at maths.”

qa.q: Why did Vasudha snap at Mira's puzzle?
qa.a: She was afraid of not seeing the answer and losing the “clever” label, so she felt angry and embarrassed.

qa.q: How could Thomas Sir or Amma praise Vasudha differently?
qa.a: Praise her effort and strategies, like trying different ways, so hard puzzles feel safe rather than dangerous.

qa.q: How might Mira feel when Vasudha calls her question stupid?
qa.a: Mira probably feels hurt and confused, since she only asked for help.

grounding: The beats show a child praised as clever beginning to avoid hard problems to protect the label, with risk feeling dangerous.

passage:
Chetan, your teachers call you a genius and you've stopped doing the hard homework. Let me, your Vidya Paati, tell you about me.
When I was nine, in Coimbatore, the whole street called me “the brain.” My father told every guest how clever I was. I loved it.
Then in Class 5 we got long-division sums that I couldn't do at first. The other children struggled too, but they tried. I didn't. I pretended I found them boring. I said I had a headache. If I didn't try, nobody could see me fail.
I got angry at the teacher, at the sums, at everyone.
It was a new teacher who said, “Vidya, I don't care if you're clever. I care that you try.” That was the first time I felt safe getting something wrong.
Don't let a word like genius stop you, kanna.

qa.q: What did the street call young Vidya?
qa.a: They called her “the brain.”

qa.q: Why did young Vidya pretend the sums were boring?
qa.a: She was afraid that failing would take away her “clever” label, so avoiding the sums felt safer; she also felt angry.

qa.q: At what point in the story did young Vidya start to feel safe trying?
qa.a: When the new teacher said she cared about trying more than cleverness.

qa.q: How might young Vidya's father have felt if he knew his praise made her afraid?
qa.a: He would probably have felt surprised and sad, since he only meant to show pride.

grounding: The grandmother's memory shows a child praised as clever avoiding hard sums to protect the label, until effort is valued instead.

passage:
It was the night before the school science fair, and the power in the colony kept flickering. Vandana, eleven, sat at the table with her aunt Uma.
Everyone called Vandana “our little scientist.” Uma always said, “You're so smart, you'll win easily.”
Her teacher had suggested a hard project: building a water filter and testing it. Vandana had chosen instead to make a poster about the planets, which she already knew by heart.
“Why not the filter?” Uma asked.
Vandana shrugged. “What if it doesn't work? Then everyone will see I'm not that smart.”
Uma paused, the torch in her hand. She thought of all the times she'd said “so smart.”
“Vandana, I think I've been saying the wrong thing. I'm proud when you try hard things. Even if they don't work.”
Vandana looked at the planets poster, then away, cheeks hot.

qa.q: What hard project had the teacher suggested?
qa.a: Building a water filter and testing it.

qa.q: Why did Vandana choose the planets poster?
qa.a: She was afraid that a failed filter would show she isn't smart, so the safe project protected her label.

qa.q: What did Uma change in how she praised Vandana?
qa.a: She said she is proud when Vandana tries hard things even if they fail, praising effort rather than being smart.

qa.q: How might Uma feel realising her praise played a part?
qa.a: Uma seems regretful and thoughtful, recognising that “so smart” made risk feel dangerous.

grounding: The passage shows a child repeatedly called smart choosing a safe project to protect the label, and an aunt rethinking her praise.

passage:
All through the Diwali holidays, Darshan mama kept saying it. When Madhav solved the riddle on the sweet box: "Genius!" When he counted the diyas fastest: "Our little scientist, so clever!" Madhav glowed.
On the last evening, the family set up a puzzle contest on the terrace. There were easy cards and hard cards, and the hard ones had a gold star.
"Take a gold one, genius," said Darshan mama.
Madhav's hand hovered. He picked an easy card instead. Then another easy one.
"Why not the hard ones?"
"These are more fun," Madhav said, not looking up.
But when his cousin grabbed a gold card and got stuck, Madhav watched him with a funny tight feeling in his stomach. If he got stuck in front of everyone, would they still call him a genius?

qa.q: Which cards had a gold star?
qa.a: The hard cards had a gold star.

qa.q: Why does Madhav pick the easy cards?
qa.a: He feels nervous that getting stuck on a hard card in front of everyone would take away the "genius" label he has been praised for.

qa.q: How could Darshan mama praise Madhav in a more helpful way?
qa.a: He could praise Madhav's effort and ways of thinking, like "I liked how you tried different ideas", so trying something hard doesn't feel risky.

qa.q: How might Darshan mama feel if he knew why Madhav avoided the gold cards?
qa.a: He would probably be surprised and a bit sorry, since he meant his praise to encourage Madhav, not to make him afraid.

grounding: It shows a child who is repeatedly called clever avoiding the hard puzzles to keep that label, as praise for traits makes risk feel dangerous.

passage:
"Gopika, try this one!" Parveen khala held up the newspaper. "The hard sudoku. You're so clever, you'll do it in five minutes."
The Eid guests had gone, and the house smelled of sheer khurma.
"I don't want to."
"Why? You're the smartest in the family!"
"I'll do the easy one."
"The easy one is for babies. You did it in two minutes yesterday."
"I like the easy one." Gopika pulled the paper toward her and folded the hard puzzle under.
"Gopika. What's wrong?"
Gopika picked at the corner of the paper. "What if I can't do the hard one? Then everyone will say I'm not clever any more."
Parveen khala was quiet. Then she sat down beside her. "Shall we try it together, and get stuck together?"

qa.q: Which sudoku did Gopika want to do?
qa.a: She wanted to do the easy one.

qa.q: Why does Gopika fold the hard puzzle under?
qa.a: She feels afraid that failing the hard one would take away her label of being clever, so avoiding it feels safer.

qa.q: What did Parveen khala do at the end, and why is it a good move?
qa.a: She offered to try the hard puzzle together and get stuck together, which makes struggle normal instead of a threat to Gopika's cleverness.

qa.q: How does Parveen khala seem to feel when Gopika explains?
qa.a: She seems surprised and thoughtful, realising her praise has made Gopika scared to try.

grounding: It shows a child who is always called clever avoiding a hard puzzle to protect that label, as praise for traits makes risk feel dangerous.

passage:
When I was nine, in the winter holidays, my Dadaji Jagdish told everyone I was the smartest child in the colony. I'm Yash, and I loved hearing it.
Then the maths olympiad came. There were two papers: normal and advanced. Dadaji said, "Of course Yash will write advanced."
I chose normal. I told him the advanced one was on the same day as my friend's birthday. That wasn't true.
The truth was that if I tried advanced and got a low score, I wouldn't be the smartest any more. It felt safer to win the easy one than lose the hard one.
I got full marks in the normal paper. Dadaji was happy. I felt strange, like I had kept something but lost something too.

qa.q: What reason did Yash give for not writing the advanced paper?
qa.a: Yash said it was on the same day as a friend's birthday, which wasn't true.

qa.q: How did Yash feel after getting full marks in the normal paper?
qa.a: Yash felt strange and uneasy, as if something was kept but something was also lost.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could have helped?
qa.a: Being praised as the smartest made Yash afraid to risk a low score; if Dadaji had praised effort and trying hard things, the advanced paper might have felt less dangerous.

qa.q: How might Dadaji have felt if he knew the real reason?
qa.a: Dadaji would likely feel surprised and sad that the praise had made the advanced paper feel frightening.

grounding: It shows a child repeatedly called the smartest avoiding the harder paper to protect that label, as praise for traits made risk feel dangerous.

passage:
Summer puzzle club, week three. Note for Preeti's family.
Preeti arrived today holding her uncle Vishal's hand; he told me again, "She's our little genius, she never gets anything wrong." Preeti smiled but went quiet.
When I put out the harder grid puzzles, Preeti chose the easy ones she had finished last week. I asked her to try a new grid. She said, "I don't want to," and when a square wouldn't fit she pushed the sheet away and scowled. Later she told me softly, "If I get it wrong, I won't be clever anymore."
Next I sat beside her and we solved one row together. I praised how she tested three numbers before one fitted. She tried a second row alone.
Suggestion: at home, notice her trying, not her being smart.

qa.q: Which puzzles did Preeti choose when the harder grids came out?
qa.a: She chose the easy ones she had finished last week.

qa.q: Why does Preeti push the sheet away and scowl?
qa.a: She feels scared and angry, because a wrong answer seems to threaten the clever label she keeps hearing, and she worries she won't be clever anymore.

qa.q: How could Preeti's family support her at home?
qa.a: They could praise the way she tries, like testing different numbers, instead of calling her a genius who never gets things wrong.

qa.q: How might Vishal see Preeti's choice of easy puzzles if he only hears about her scores?
qa.a: Vishal might think she is simply doing well, without noticing that the genius label is making her avoid anything hard.

grounding: A child repeatedly called clever starts avoiding harder puzzles to protect that label, as seen by the adult running the club.
